sessions.title: Mathematical statements, truth values & predicates
sessions.purpose: Build mathematical statements, truth values & predicates as an independently observable capability before later probability/research modules.
sessions.centralCapability: Distinguish a truth-evaluable statement from an expression/question. Determine a closed statement's truth value. Distinguish an open predicate from a closed statement. Identify a predicate's free variable. Evaluate a predicate at a supplied input.
sessions.principalObstacle: Avoid the characteristic shortcut/category error for mathematical statements, truth values & predicates.
requiredOwnership: Distinguish a truth-evaluable statement from an expression/question.
Determine a closed statement's truth value.
Distinguish an open predicate from a closed statement.
Evaluate a predicate at a supplied input.
sessions.transferScope: Changed-surface transfer: the same owned capability must be reconstructed on a materially different representation or context.

sessions.lesson: A statement is a complete sentence that is true or false; expressions and questions are not statements, while a predicate becomes closed only after its free variable is supplied or quantified. Worked example: “9 is odd” is a true statement; “u+7” is an expression; “u>7” is a predicate. Guided check: Classify “2+5=8”, “v²−1”, and “v²=1”, then evaluate the predicate at v=1 and v=3.

sessions.lesson: P→Q fails only at P=true,Q=false. Converse is Q→P; inverse ¬P→¬Q; contrapositive ¬Q→¬P; original and contrapositive are equivalent. Worked example: x>6→x>2 is true over reals, but the converse fails at x=4. Guided check: Write all four forms of x<−1→x<3.

sessions.principalObstacle: Avoid the characteristic shortcut/category error for biconditionals; necessary & sufficient conditions.
requiredOwnership: Distinguish necessary from sufficient when reverse fails.
Establish/refute iff by checking both directions.
sessions.transferScope: Proof reconstruction on a related instance; the proof architecture is taught and must be executed correctly.

sessions.lesson: P↔Q means both P→Q and Q→P. If P→Q, then P is sufficient for Q and Q is necessary for P; the reverse direction must be checked separately. Worked example: over integers, 4|n implies n is even, so divisibility by4 is sufficient for evenness and evenness is necessary for divisibility by4. The reverse fails, for example at n=6. Guided check: compare “n is divisible by6” with “n is divisible by3”; check both arrows and give a counterexample to any failed direction.

sessions.centralCapability: Track and explain the stated quantifier domain. Interpret universal quantification. Interpret existential quantification. Use a witness for an existential. Use a counterexample against a universal.
sessions.principalObstacle: Avoid the characteristic shortcut/category error for universal & existential quantifiers.
requiredOwnership: Track and explain the stated quantifier domain.
Use a witness for an existential.
Use a counterexample against a universal.
sessions.transferScope: Retrieval/fluency on a new instance; the underlying method is already explicit in instruction.
sessions.exitCondition: Solve Main and Transfer while visibly satisfying the five ownership claims for Universal & existential quantifiers.
sessions.lesson: ∀ requires every legal value in the stated domain; ∃ requires at least one. A witness establishes an existential; one legal counterexample refutes a universal. Worked example: over integers, ∃n(n²=25) is true because n=5 is a witness, while ∀n(n+1>n) is true because adding1 increases every integer. Guided check: on the domain {0,1,2,3}, decide ∀m(m<4) and ∃m(m²=4), explicitly naming the domain before deciding.

sessions.principalObstacle: Avoid the characteristic shortcut/category error for negating quantified claims correctly.
requiredOwnership: Translate the exact negation to ordinary language.
sessions.transferScope: Changed-surface transfer: the same owned capability must be reconstructed on a materially different representation or context.
sessions.exitCondition: Solve Main and Transfer while visibly satisfying the five ownership claims for Negating quantified claims correctly.
sessions.lesson: Negation switches ∀↔∃, negates the predicate, and keeps the same domain. The negation of u>3 is u≤3. Worked example: The negation of 'every real x has x²>1' is 'some real x has x²≤1.' Guided check: Negate 'there exists an integer n with n<−4.'

sessions.title: Quantifier order & witness dependence
sessions.focus: Nested quantifiers, scope and allowed dependence
sessions.purpose: Make nested quantifier order operational before later proof and analysis modules require parameter-dependent choices.
sessions.centralCapability: Read, construct, negate and refute two-quantifier claims while tracking which choices may depend on earlier quantified variables.
sessions.principalObstacle: Treating ∀x∃y and ∃y∀x as interchangeable, or using a witness chosen after x when the claim requires one witness chosen before x.
entryPrerequisites: M03-S05 universal/existential quantifiers over stated domains
M03-S06 exact negation of quantified claims
requiredOwnership: Read nested ∀∃ and ∃∀ claims in the stated order over explicit domains.
Explain when an existential witness may depend on an earlier universally quantified variable.
Distinguish input-dependent witnesses from one global witness that must work for every input.
Negate a two-quantifier claim by switching each quantifier, preserving domains and complementing the predicate.
Refute a false quantifier order with a legal adversarial choice made after the proposed global witness.
sessions.applicationScope: Elementary quantified claims over integers and finite assignment relations; no limit notation.
sessions.transferScope: Changed-surface transfer: reconstruct dependence as a finite assignment/function problem rather than an inequality over integers.
outOfScope: epsilon-N or epsilon-delta definitions until M09
uniform convergence or advanced analysis terminology
choice axioms or infinite selection theorems
sessions.exitCondition: Solve the integer Main and finite-assignment Transfer while explicitly identifying who is chosen first, who may depend on whom, and why the reversed order succeeds or fails.
sessions.lesson: A quantified sentence is read in order. In ∀x∈X ∃y∈Y P(x,y), x is chosen first; after seeing that x, you may choose a y that can depend on x. A useful way to record this is y=f(x). In ∃y∈Y ∀x∈X P(x,y), y is chosen first, so the same y must survive every legal x; it may not be changed after x is revealed. To negate nested quantifiers, switch each quantifier and negate the final predicate while keeping the same domains: ¬(∀x∈X ∃y∈Y P(x,y)) is ∃x∈X ∀y∈Y ¬P(x,y), and ¬(∃y∈Y ∀x∈X P(x,y)) is ∀y∈Y ∃x∈X ¬P(x,y). Worked example: over integers, consider ∀n∈Z ∃k∈Z with k=n+2. It is true: once n is given, choose k=n+2. The reversed claim ∃k∈Z ∀n∈Z with k=n+2 is false: after a fixed k is proposed, choosing n=k makes the required equality k=k+2 impossible. The lesson is not that ∀∃ is always true or ∃∀ is always false; the predicate decides truth, while the quantifier order decides what dependence is allowed. Guided check: over real numbers, compare ∀x∈R ∃y∈R with y=3x−1 and ∃y∈R ∀x∈R with y=3x−1. For the first, write a witness rule. For the second, explain what a single y would have to do and give one x-choice that defeats a proposed y.

sessions.title: Counterexamples, boundary cases & claim debugging
sessions.purpose: Build counterexample search into a complete debugging cycle: refute a false universal claim, repair it economically, and prove the repaired theorem.
sessions.centralCapability: Search strategically for a legal counterexample, verify the failure, repair the false statement without gratuitous boundary changes, and prove the repaired claim.
sessions.principalObstacle: Stopping after a counterexample or treating a plausible repaired statement as true because it survives a few tests.
requiredOwnership: Search strategically near sign, zero or domain boundaries and verify counterexample legality/hypotheses.
Verify conclusion failure and use one legal counterexample to refute a universal implication.
Explain why confirming examples do not prove a universal claim.
Repair a false statement while preserving the original domain/hypothesis unless a change is explicitly justified.
Prove the repaired statement rather than merely testing additional examples.
sessions.applicationScope: Elementary real/integer universal claims whose failure can be diagnosed and repaired with already-owned algebra.
sessions.transferScope: Changed-surface transfer: move from search/refutation on an inequality to refute→repair→prove on a zero-product implication.
outOfScope: Polynomial-inequality theory not owned by M01
sessions.exitCondition: Independently refute the Main claim and, on Transfer, refute a different false statement, repair it and prove the repaired theorem.
sessions.lesson: A mathematical counterexample must be legal, satisfy every hypothesis and make the conclusion false. One such example refutes a universal statement; many confirming examples do not prove it. Debugging should then continue: repair the statement as economically as possible and prove the repair. Worked example: over integers, the claim 6|n⇒4|n is false because n=6 satisfies 6|n but not 4|n. A useful repair is 6|n⇒3|n. If 6|n, then n=6k=3(2k) for some integer k, so the repaired conclusion follows for every legal n. Guided check: audit 10|n⇒6|n. Find a legal counterexample, propose a divisor conclusion that really follows from 10|n, and write the witness form you would use to prove your repaired claim. Search first near small multiples and divisor boundaries; do not call a repair proved until the universal argument is complete.

sessions.lesson: For integers, a|b means b=ak for some integer k. Even integers are2k and odd integers2k+1; negative divisors use the same definition. Worked example: 7|−35 with witness−5, while6∤25. Guided check: Give witnesses for−3|18 and8|56.

sessions.title: Direct proof architecture
sessions.purpose: Build direct proof architecture as an independently observable capability before later probability/research modules.
sessions.centralCapability: Start with arbitrary objects satisfying hypotheses. Unpack definitions. Derive symbolically. Match the target definition. Explain why examples are not universal proof.
sessions.principalObstacle: Avoid the characteristic shortcut/category error for direct proof architecture.
requiredOwnership: Start with arbitrary objects satisfying hypotheses.
Explain why examples are not universal proof.
sessions.transferScope: Proof reconstruction on a related instance; the proof architecture is taught and must be executed correctly.
sessions.exitCondition: Solve Main and Transfer while visibly satisfying the five ownership claims for Direct proof architecture.
sessions.lesson: A direct proof of a universal implication starts with arbitrary legal objects satisfying the hypotheses, unpacks definitions, derives symbolically, and finishes by matching the conclusion definition. Worked example: if n is odd, then n+2 is odd. Write n=2k+1 for some integer k; then n+2=2(k+1)+1, which has the required odd form. Guided check: if 6|n, unpack the divisibility witness and show directly that n is even, naming the integer witness that matches the even definition. Search discipline: scratchwork and final proof have different jobs. In scratchwork, write the givens and the target definition, work backward from the target to identify a useful witness or intermediate statement, and allow failed routes. Once the connection is found, the final proof should start from arbitrary legal givens and present only the justified forward logical spine. Working backward is a discovery device, not permission to assume the conclusion.

sessions.title: Constructive existence & uniqueness
sessions.purpose: Separate constructing a legal object from proving that no other legal object can satisfy the same property.
sessions.centralCapability: Prove elementary existence-and-uniqueness claims by constructing and verifying a witness, then proving uniqueness as a separate obligation.
sessions.principalObstacle: Treating an algebraic candidate as automatic existence, or treating one found solution as proof that no second solution exists.
requiredOwnership: Decompose an exactly-one claim into existence and at-most-one obligations.
Construct a candidate and verify both its domain membership and the original defining property.
Prove uniqueness by taking two arbitrary legal objects with the property and showing they are equal.
Distinguish at-least-one, at-most-one and exactly-one conclusions.
Audit how changing the domain can preserve existence while changing uniqueness.
sessions.applicationScope: Elementary algebraic objects over explicit real or restricted-real domains.
sessions.transferScope: Changed-surface transfer: move from an affine parameter equation to a nonlinear equation whose uniqueness changes with the domain.
sessions.exitCondition: Produce a checked witness and a separate uniqueness proof, then correctly diagnose a domain change that alters uniqueness.
sessions.lesson: The symbol ∃! means exactly one, and an exactly-one proof has two logically separate jobs. Existence: construct at least one legal object and check it in the original domain and property. Uniqueness: assume u and v are any two legal objects with the property and prove u=v. A solver output or transformed equation is only a candidate until it is checked against the original conditions. Worked example: fix a real parameter t. For 5x−2t=9, the candidate x=(9+2t)/5 is real and substitution verifies existence. If u and v both satisfy the equation, then 5u−2t=9=5v−2t, hence 5u=5v and u=v, proving uniqueness. Guided check: for a real parameter c, solve 3x+c=12, verify the candidate in the original equation, then write a one-line two-solution uniqueness argument. Finally say which line proves existence and which proves at most one.

sessions.title: Proof by contraposition
sessions.purpose: Build proof by contraposition as an independently observable capability before later probability/research modules.
sessions.centralCapability: Write the exact contrapositive. Use logical equivalence correctly. Prove the contrapositive. Avoid proving the converse. Reconnect to the original implication.
sessions.principalObstacle: Avoid the characteristic shortcut/category error for proof by contraposition.
sessions.transferScope: Proof reconstruction on a related instance; the proof architecture is taught and must be executed correctly.
sessions.exitCondition: Solve Main and Transfer while visibly satisfying the five ownership claims for Proof by contraposition.
sessions.lesson: To prove P→Q by contraposition, prove the logically equivalent ¬Q→¬P; proving Q→P would be the converse, not the same theorem. Worked example: Prove “if n² is odd, then n is odd.” Its contrapositive is “if n is even, then n² is even.” Write n=2k; then n²=4k²=2(2k²), so the contrapositive holds and therefore the original implication holds. Guided check: For |x|<3→x²<9, write the contrapositive exactly and identify which inequality endpoints change under negation.

sessions.title: Proof by contradiction
sessions.purpose: Build proof by contradiction as an independently observable capability before later probability/research modules.
sessions.centralCapability: Assume the negation. Derive consequences. Identify an impossibility. Discharge the assumption. Distinguish contradiction from failed search.
sessions.principalObstacle: Avoid the characteristic shortcut/category error for proof by contradiction.
sessions.transferScope: Proof reconstruction on a related instance; the proof architecture is taught and must be executed correctly.
sessions.exitCondition: Solve Main and Transfer while visibly satisfying the five ownership claims for Proof by contradiction.
sessions.lesson: A contradiction proof assumes the exact negation of the target, derives consequences using valid steps, reaches an explicit impossibility, and then rejects the assumption. Failed search is not a contradiction. Worked example: There is no smallest positive rational number. If r>0 were the smallest positive rational, then r/2 would also be a positive rational and would satisfy 0<r/2<r, contradicting minimality. Guided check: Assume there is a largest negative rational q and use q/2 to identify the contradiction.

sessions.title: Remainder classes & exhaustive proof cases
sessions.purpose: Build remainder classes & exhaustive proof cases as an independently observable capability before later probability/research modules.
sessions.centralCapability: Write n=dq+r with0≤r<d. List all small remainder classes. Prove every exhaustive case. Recombine into a universal result. Distinguish exhaustive proof from finite examples.
sessions.principalObstacle: Avoid the characteristic shortcut/category error for remainder classes & exhaustive proof cases.
requiredOwnership: Distinguish exhaustive proof from finite examples.
sessions.transferScope: Proof reconstruction on a related instance; the proof architecture is taught and must be executed correctly.
sessions.exitCondition: Solve Main and Transfer while visibly satisfying the five ownership claims for Remainder classes & exhaustive proof cases.
sessions.lesson: For positive d, every integer has exactly one form n=dq+r with 0≤r<d. An exhaustive case proof lists every possible r and proves the claim symbolically in each case; checking a few numerical inputs is not the same thing. Worked example: Every integer square has remainder 0 or 1 on division by 3. If n=3q, n²=9q²; if n=3q+1, n²=3(3q²+2q)+1; if n=3q+2, n²=3(3q²+4q+1)+1. These three cases exhaust the integers. Guided check: Using the two parity forms n=2q and n=2q+1, show that n³ has the same parity as n.

sessions.title: Mathematical induction
sessions.purpose: Build mathematical induction as an independently observable capability before later probability/research modules.
sessions.centralCapability: State induction domain/start. Verify base case. State induction hypothesis. Use it in k+1 step. Conclude by induction.
sessions.principalObstacle: Avoid the characteristic shortcut/category error for mathematical induction.
sessions.transferScope: Proof reconstruction on a related instance; the proof architecture is taught and must be executed correctly.
sessions.exitCondition: Solve Main and Transfer while visibly satisfying the five ownership claims for Mathematical induction.
sessions.lesson: Ordinary induction proves an integer-indexed claim by verifying the first case, assuming the claim for an arbitrary k, and using that exact hypothesis to derive the k+1 case. Worked example: prove 7|(8^n−1) for n≥1. The base n=1 gives 8−1=7. Assume 8^k−1=7q for some integer q; then 8^(k+1)−1=8(8^k−1)+7=7(8q+1), so the next case follows. Guided check: for 1+2+⋯+n=n(n+1)/2, state the base case, induction hypothesis, and exact k+1 target, but do not finish the algebra.

sessions.title: Strong induction & recursive claims
sessions.purpose: Build strong induction & recursive claims as an independently observable capability before later probability/research modules.
sessions.centralCapability: Verify all required bases. State an all-prior hypothesis. Reduce target to earlier covered cases. Avoid circularity. Explain why strong induction fits.
sessions.principalObstacle: Avoid the characteristic shortcut/category error for strong induction & recursive claims.
requiredOwnership: Reduce target to earlier covered cases.
sessions.transferScope: Proof reconstruction on a related instance; the proof architecture is taught and must be executed correctly.
sessions.exitCondition: Solve Main and Transfer while visibly satisfying the five ownership claims for Strong induction & recursive claims.
sessions.lesson: Strong induction assumes every earlier case from the starting index through k, which is useful when the next case reduces to more than one possible earlier value. Worked example: every integer n≥2 is either prime or a product of primes. Base n=2 is prime. Assume the statement holds for every integer from2 through k. For k+1, if it is prime we are done; if it is composite, write k+1=ab with 2≤a,b≤k, apply the all-prior hypothesis to a and b, and combine their prime factorizations. Guided check: if a future target P(n) naturally reduces to a case P(m) with m<n but not necessarily m=n−1, explain why an all-prior hypothesis is useful and what must be true of the base range.

sessions.title: Well-ordering, least counterexamples & finite extrema
sessions.purpose: Connect induction-style reduction to the legal choice of a least integer counterexample and to justified extremal choices in finite sets.
sessions.centralCapability: Use well-ordering or finiteness to choose a legitimate extremal object, then reduce it to a smaller legal case or contradiction.
sessions.principalObstacle: Writing 'take the smallest counterexample' without proving a smallest element exists, especially when the domain is not the nonnegative integers or a finite set.
requiredOwnership: State the well-ordering principle for nonempty subsets of the nonnegative integers.
Define a nonempty counterexample set before selecting a least counterexample.
Reduce a supposed least counterexample to a smaller legal case and derive a contradiction.
Reject an unjustified claim that every nonempty set of real numbers has a minimum.
Choose and use a justified extremal element of a nonempty finite set.
sessions.applicationScope: Elementary integer claims and bounded finite extremal arguments.
sessions.transferScope: Changed-surface transfer: move from least-counterexample proof of an indexed inequality to an extremal argument on an arbitrary finite set.
sessions.exitCondition: Use a least counterexample only after establishing its legal existence, and separately justify a finite extremal choice without overgeneralizing to arbitrary real sets.
sessions.lesson: Well-ordering says every nonempty subset of the nonnegative integers has a least element. A least-counterexample proof therefore has obligations: define the counterexample set, assume it is nonempty, choose its least member N, verify N is not a protected base case, and use the failure at N to produce a smaller legal counterexample or a contradiction. This principle is about nonnegative integers; it does not say every nonempty set of real numbers has a minimum. For example, the positive reals have no least element because x/2 is smaller than any proposed x>0. A nonempty finite set of reals does have a minimum, so finite extremal choices are also legitimate. Worked example: prove 3 divides 4^n−1 for every integer n≥1 by least counterexample. If C were nonempty, let N be its least element. N≠1 because 4−1=3. Then N−1 is not a counterexample, so 3 divides 4^(N−1)−1. Since 4^N−1=4(4^(N−1)−1)+3, the N case is also divisible by 3, contradiction. Guided check: outline the same least-counterexample obligations for the claim 2^n≥n+1 for n≥0 without completing the final algebra; explicitly name the counterexample set and explain why a least element exists.

sessions.title: Union, intersection, difference & complement
sessions.purpose: Build union, intersection, difference & complement as an independently observable capability before later probability/research modules.

entryPrerequisites: JIT set-operation definitions in this lesson

sessions.lesson: For subsets of a stated universe U, A∪B contains elements in A or B, A∩B contains elements in both, A\B contains elements in A but not B, and A^c contains the elements of U outside A. Complement therefore depends on the chosen universe. Worked example: Let U={1,2,3,4,5}, A={1,3,5}, B={3,4}. Then A∪B={1,3,4,5}, A∩B={3}, A\B={1,5}, B\A={4}, and A^c={2,4}. Guided check: With U={0,1,2,3,4}, C={0,2,4}, D={2,3}, compute C∪D, C∩D, C\D and C^c.

sessions.lesson: To prove two sets X and Y are equal, take an arbitrary element x and prove x∈X iff x∈Y; the iff chain establishes both containments at once. Also, x∈A\B means x∈A and x∉B. Worked example: Prove (A∩B)^c=A^c∪B^c. For arbitrary x, x∈(A∩B)^c iff x∉A∩B iff x∉A or x∉B iff x∈A^c or x∈B^c iff x∈A^c∪B^c. Guided check: Prove (A^c)^c=A elementwise by starting from an arbitrary x and writing an iff chain.

sessions.lesson: A Cartesian product A×B contains ordered pairs (a,b), so (a,b) and (b,a) are generally different objects. A relation from A to B is any subset of A×B; it is a function only when every input in A occurs with exactly one output. Worked example: {1,2}×{p,q}={(1,p),(1,q),(2,p),(2,q)}. The relation {(1,p),(2,q)} is a function from {1,2} to {p,q}, whereas {(1,p),(1,q)} is not because input 1 has two outputs. Guided check: Build {u,v}×{0,1,2} and give one relation on it that is a function and one that is not.

sessions.lesson: For f:A→B, A is the domain and B the codomain; the range is only the codomain values actually hit. For S⊆A, f(S) is the image of S. For T⊆B, f⁻¹(T) means all inputs whose outputs lie in T and does not require f to have an inverse function. Worked example: Let h:{p,q,r}→{0,1,2,3} satisfy h(p)=1,h(q)=1,h(r)=3. The range is {1,3}; h({p,r})={1,3}; h⁻¹({1})={p,q}; 0 and 2 are codomain values outside the range. Guided check: For k:{a,b,c,d}→{x,y,z} with a,b↦x, c↦y, d↦z, find the range and the preimage of {x,z}.

sessions.lesson: Injective means distinct inputs never collide; surjective means every codomain value is hit; bijective means both and is exactly the finite-map situation in which a two-sided inverse can undo the map in both directions. Worked example: Let h:{1,2}→{a,b,c} with h(1)=a,h(2)=b. It is injective but not surjective because c is never hit, so no two-sided inverse h⁻¹:{a,b,c}→{1,2} can satisfy h∘h⁻¹=id on the whole codomain. Guided check: Classify the map {u,v,w}→{0,1,2} given u↦2,v↦0,w↦1, and if possible write its inverse.

sessions.purpose: Build equivalence relations & partitions as an independently observable capability before later probability/research modules.

sessions.principalObstacle: Avoid the characteristic shortcut/category error for equivalence relations & partitions.
entryPrerequisites: JIT equivalence-relation definitions in this lesson
requiredOwnership: Conclude equivalence only after all three.
sessions.transferScope: Proof reconstruction on a related instance; the proof architecture is taught and must be executed correctly.
sessions.exitCondition: Solve Main and Transfer while visibly satisfying the five ownership claims for Equivalence relations & partitions.
sessions.lesson: For a relation R on a set D: reflexive means ∀x∈D, xRx; symmetric means ∀x,y∈D, xRy⇒yRx; transitive means ∀x,y,z∈D, (xRy and yRz)⇒xRz. Only when all three hold is R an equivalence relation. The class [x]={y∈D:yRx}; equivalence classes cover D and any two classes are either identical or disjoint, so they form a partition. Worked example: On D={11,12,21,22}, define xRy when x and y have the same last digit. Reflexivity holds because every number has its own last digit; symmetry holds because “same last digit” is symmetric; transitivity holds because if x and y, then y and z, have the same last digit, x and z do too. The classes are {11,21} and {12,22}. Guided check: On {p,q,r}, verify that ordinary equality is an equivalence relation and list its classes.

sessions.lesson: Use addition for disjoint alternative branches and multiplication for sequential stages. If alternative branches overlap, direct addition double-counts and needs correction. Worked example: choosing the first coordinate from {α,β} and the second coordinate from {1,2,3,4,5} gives 2·5 ordered pairs by the product rule. Separately, if E={2,4,6,8} and O={1,3,5} are disjoint, then |E∪O|=4+3=7 by the addition rule. Guided check: a path chooses one of3 gates and then one of4 rooms; separately, two disjoint boxes contain5 and2 objects. Identify which count is sequential and which is alternative before calculating.

sessions.lesson: For n distinct objects, n!=n(n−1)⋯1 counts all orderings. Filling r labeled positions without replacement gives P(n,r)=n!/(n−r)! because the available choices decrease at every stage. Worked example: five runners can receive gold, silver and bronze in 5·4·3=P(5,3)=60 ways; the medal labels make the order matter. Guided check: from eight candidates, count the ordered choices for captain and deputy as 8·7=P(8,2), and explain why reversing the two people gives a different assignment.

sessions.title: Bijections, encodings & uniform fibres
sessions.focus: Reversible finite representations and justified division
sessions.purpose: Turn 'same number of objects' and 'divide the overcount' into explicit mapping arguments with checked inverses or constant fibre sizes.
sessions.centralCapability: Build a reversible encoding or audit a finite many-to-one map by inspecting its fibres before transferring counts.
sessions.principalObstacle: Treating an intuitive correspondence as automatically bijective, or dividing by a supposed symmetry factor without proving every counted object has the same number of preimages.
requiredOwnership: Define an explicit finite encoding map between two collections.
Construct and verify an inverse map to prove a counting correspondence is bijective.
Transfer a finite count through a proved bijection without losing or duplicating objects.
Interpret a fibre as the preimage of one output under a finite map.
Use division by a multiplicity only after proving all relevant fibres have the same positive size, and detect when that condition fails.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite sets, strings, functions and many-to-one counting maps.
sessions.transferScope: Changed-surface transfer: audit a tempting divide-by-three argument by discovering variable fibre sizes in a marked-string map.
sessions.exitCondition: Prove one count by a reversible encoding and correctly reject a division argument whose fibre multiplicity is not constant.
sessions.lesson: A counting encoding is trustworthy when the map is explicit and reversible. To prove a finite map φ:A→B is a bijection, define how an object of A is encoded, define a reverse map ψ:B→A, and check that applying one after the other returns the original object. For a many-to-one map, the fibre over b∈B is φ⁻¹({b}), the set of inputs that map to b. If every b has exactly the same positive number q of preimages, then A is partitioned into equal fibres and |A|=q|B|. Division by q is legal only after this constant-fibre fact is proved. Worked example: a function f:{1,2,3}→{A,B} can be encoded as the three-letter string f(1)f(2)f(3); reading the three positions gives the inverse map, so the correspondence is bijective and there are 2^3 such functions. For a constant-fibre contrast, the absolute-value map from {−4,−3,−2,−1,1,2,3,4} onto {1,2,3,4} has exactly two preimages over each output. Guided check: for the map that forgets the sign from {−3,−2,−1,1,2,3} to {1,2,3}, list every fibre and explain why division by 2 is justified.

sessions.lesson: If swapping identical copies changes nothing visible, n! overcounts and internal repeat factorials must be divided out. Worked example: AABC has4!/2!=12 distinct strings. Guided check: count AABB arrangements. Labeled-group bridge: if n distinct objects are split into labeled groups of fixed sizes n1,…,nk with n1+⋯+nk=n, first imagine a temporary ordering of all n objects. There are n! such orders. Within each labeled group, however, its n_i! internal rearrangements do not change the assignment, so divide them out. Therefore the number of labeled-group assignments is n!/(n1!⋯nk!). The group labels remain distinct and are not divided out. For example, assigning6 distinct cards to labeled boxes A(2),B(1),C(3) gives6!/(2!1!3!) assignments.

sessions.title: Combinations, binomial coefficients, subsets & binomial expansion
sessions.focus: Combinations, subsets and the binomial theorem coefficients.
sessions.purpose: Own combinations as subset counts, preserve the ordered↔unordered counting bridge, and establish the finite binomial theorem strongly enough for M10's arbitrary-positive-integer power-rule proof.
sessions.centralCapability: Use nCr as a subset count, exploit symmetry, connect ordered and unordered selections, and state/use the finite binomial theorem with a combinatorial explanation of C(n,k).
sessions.principalObstacle: Treating nCr as an isolated formula—or treating one rehearsed expansion as ownership of the general finite binomial theorem—hides the counting structure later proofs consume.
requiredOwnership: State and use the finite binomial theorem for positive integer n, and explain combinatorially why the coefficient of x^(n−k)y^k is C(n,k).
sessions.transferScope: Retrieval/fluency on a new instance; the underlying method is already explicit in instruction.
sessions.exitCondition: State the finite binomial theorem for positive integer n, justify its coefficient C(n,k) by factor-choice counting, and apply it on a fresh finite expansion while retaining the subset/complement interpretation of combinations.
sessions.lesson: A combination selects an r-element subset, so internal order is irrelevant: C(n,r)=n!/[r!(n−r)!]. An ordered r-selection can be built in two stages: first choose the r-element subset in C(n,r) ways, then order its r chosen elements in r! ways. Therefore P(n,r)=C(n,r)·r!, which explains the factorial formula rather than treating division by r! as a cancellation trick. Choosing the included r items is symmetric with choosing the excluded n−r items, so C(n,r)=C(n,n−r). The same subset-counting idea gives the finite binomial theorem. In the product of n factors (x+y), a term x^(n−k)y^k is produced by choosing exactly which k of the n factors contribute y; there are C(n,k) such choices. Hence for every positive integer n, (x+y)^n=Σ(k=0..n) C(n,k)x^(n−k)y^k. Worked example: (x+y)^3=x³+3x²y+3xy²+y³ because the coefficients are C(3,0),C(3,1),C(3,2),C(3,3). Guided check: in (p+q)^6, do not expand the whole expression. Explain why the coefficient of p^4q^2 is C(6,2)=15 by choosing which two factors contribute q, and connect that choice-count to the general coefficient C(n,k).

sessions.title: Double counting & combinatorial identities
sessions.focus: One finite set counted in two valid ways
sessions.purpose: Turn algebraic counting identities into explanations by defining one finite collection and decomposing it in two independent ways.
sessions.centralCapability: Define a finite incidence/pair set, count the same objects exactly once in two ways, and equate the results.
sessions.principalObstacle: Equating two expressions because they look algebraically similar without proving that both count the same finite objects under compatible boundary conventions.
requiredOwnership: Define one finite incidence or pair set that both sides of a counting identity enumerate.
Partition and count that set by one feature without omissions or overlap.
Count the same set by a different feature and justify that every object is counted exactly once.
Equate the two counts and state the summation/boundary conventions used.
Invent a combinatorial interpretation for an algebraic-looking finite sum using already-owned finite objects.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite subsets, incidences, marked objects and binomial sums.
sessions.transferScope: Changed-surface transfer: invent a nested-subset interpretation for a binomial-power sum instead of being given the counted incidence set.
sessions.exitCondition: Derive one identity from an explicitly supplied incidence set and independently invent a valid two-way counting model for a new finite sum.
sessions.lesson: Double counting proves an equality by counting one finite set of objects in two different valid ways. The key obligation is sameness: both calculations must count exactly the same objects, exactly once. Worked example: with five people, let I be the incidences (p,T) where T is a two-person team and p is a member of T. Counting by teams gives 2·C(5,2). Counting by the marked person gives 5·4 because after choosing p there are four choices for the teammate. Therefore 2C(5,2)=20=5·4. This is not two unrelated computations; both count I. Guided check: define incidences (p,T) for six people and three-person teams, then write—but do not simplify—the count by teams and the count by the marked person. State why each incidence appears once in each decomposition.

sessions.purpose: Build stars-and-bars: combinations with repetition as an independently observable capability before later probability/research modules.

sessions.exitCondition: Solve Main and Transfer while visibly satisfying the five ownership claims for Stars-and-bars: combinations with repetition.
sessions.lesson: Stars-and-bars encodes a nonnegative solution x1+⋯+xk=n by writing n identical stars and k−1 separators; the numbers of stars between separators are x1,…,xk. This is a bijection: every distribution gives one string and every string gives one distribution, so choosing the separator positions among n+k−1 positions gives C(n+k−1,k−1). Worked example: Five identical tokens in three labeled boxes can be written ★★|★|★★ for (2,1,2). There are 5 stars and 2 bars, so C(7,2)=21 distributions. If each box must be nonempty, reserve one token per box first. Guided check: Encode all nonnegative solutions of x+y=4 with four stars and one bar, and verify there are C(5,1)=5.

sessions.purpose: Build complement counting & inclusion-exclusion as an independently observable capability before later probability/research modules.
sessions.centralCapability: Use two-set inclusion-exclusion. Explain overlap subtraction. Use complement to count neither. Compute exactly-one counts. Apply inclusion-exclusion to divisibility counting.

sessions.transferScope: Changed-surface transfer: the same owned capability must be reconstructed on a materially different representation or context.

sessions.lesson: For two finite sets, |A∪B|=|A|+|B|−|A∩B| because naive addition counts each overlap element twice. Worked example: let A={1,2,3,4} and B={3,4,5}. Listing gives A∪B={1,2,3,4,5}; the count 4+3 overcounts the two shared elements, so 4+3−2=5. Guided check: with X={a,b,c} and Y={c,d}, list X∪Y and explain exactly which element naive addition counts twice; then, in a six-element universe where |X∪Y|=4, determine how many elements lie outside the union. Bridge for later synthesis: derive the three-set rule by adding C to A∪B. Since |(A∪B)∩C|=|A∩C|+|B∩C|−|A∩B∩C|, substitution gives |A∪B∪C|=|A|+|B|+|C|−|A∩B|−|A∩C|−|B∩C|+|A∩B∩C|.

sessions.purpose: Build pigeonhole principle as an independently observable capability before later probability/research modules.
sessions.centralCapability: Identify pigeons and holes. Force collision with more pigeons than holes. Use generalized ceiling bound. Design non-obvious holes. Explain existence-not-identity.
sessions.principalObstacle: Avoid the characteristic shortcut/category error for pigeonhole principle.
entryPrerequisites: JIT ceiling notation in this lesson
requiredOwnership: Force collision with more pigeons than holes.
sessions.transferScope: Changed-surface transfer: the same owned capability must be reconstructed on a materially different representation or context.
sessions.exitCondition: Solve Main and Transfer while visibly satisfying the five ownership claims for Pigeonhole principle.
sessions.lesson: The pigeonhole principle says that if N objects are placed into k boxes, some box contains at least ⌈N/k⌉ objects, where ⌈x⌉ is the least integer greater than or equal to x. If every box held at most ⌈N/k⌉−1, the total capacity would be too small. The theorem proves that a collision exists, not which box contains it. Worked example: Put 17 files into 4 folders. Since ⌈17/4⌉=5, one folder has at least 5 files; otherwise four folders with at most 4 files each could hold only 16. Guided check: Ten socks are placed into three drawers. State the guaranteed occupancy and justify it by the same capacity argument.

sessions.title: Invariants, integer ranks & termination
sessions.focus: State transitions, preserved quantities and decreasing integer measures
sessions.purpose: Introduce a mathematical language for proving impossibility and finite termination before M08 turns the same ideas into program invariants and loop variants.
sessions.centralCapability: Model a discrete process by states and legal moves, prove an invariant across all moves, and use a strictly decreasing nonnegative integer rank to prove termination.
sessions.principalObstacle: Assuming a preserved property proves reachability or termination, or assuming an arbitrary decreasing real quantity must force a finite process.
requiredOwnership: Define the state space, legal moves, initial state and target/terminal condition of a finite process.
Propose and prove an invariant by checking it initially and after every legal move.
Use an invariant to rule out a target without claiming that every invariant-compatible target is reachable.
Choose a nonnegative integer rank that strictly decreases at every legal move and use it to prove termination.
Distinguish termination from identification of the terminal state, and combine an invariant with termination when needed.
sessions.applicationScope: Elementary finite/discrete processes with explicitly stated legal moves.
sessions.transferScope: Changed-surface transfer: combine a preserved difference with a decreasing integer rank in a two-pile process and use the invariant to identify the terminal state.
sessions.exitCondition: Prove one target impossible by an invariant and solve a different terminating process using both an invariant and a valid nonnegative integer rank.
sessions.lesson: A state records all information needed to describe the process at one moment; a legal move specifies which transitions are allowed. An invariant is a property true in the initial state and preserved by every legal move. It can rule out any target that violates the property, but preservation alone does not prove that every other target is reachable and does not prove termination. A rank for termination is a nonnegative integer attached to each state that strictly decreases after every legal move. Such a rank cannot decrease forever, so an infinite legal sequence is impossible. The integer condition matters: a positive real quantity can decrease forever through 1,1/2,1/4,… without reaching zero in finitely many steps. Worked example: a board state is (x,y)∈Z² and a move sends (x,y) to (x+1,y−1); x+y is invariant because the +1 and −1 cancel. Separately, if a process on a nonnegative integer n replaces n by n−2 whenever n≥2, the rank n strictly decreases and proves termination. Guided check: a list operation replaces two adjacent entries by their sum. Identify one preserved numerical quantity and one nonnegative integer rank that strictly decreases, but do not infer the final value until you state the terminal rule.

sessions.purpose: Observe whether the learner can independently select a finite representation and combine previously owned proof/counting tools after all 35 earlier learner positions.
sessions.centralCapability: Define the objects, choose and justify a representation/method without a supplied label, combine multiple owned tools, audit edge/overlap conditions, and communicate a complete argument.

Select and justify a useful representation or method without a method label being supplied.

sessions.lesson: A synthesis problem should begin before a formula is chosen. First define the objects, target and constraints; then ask which representation makes the obstruction or count visible. Scratchwork may try more than one route, but the final solution should state why each chosen tool applies and how the stages fit together. Worked example: count length-4 binary strings that are not constant. The objects are the 2^4 binary strings; exactly two are constant, so the desired count is 2^4−2. The same objects can be viewed as functions from four labelled positions to {0,1}, which checks that the representation is faithful. Guided check: consider 3-person committees chosen from seven people with the requirement that at least one of two named people serves. Before calculating, state a natural universe and a complementary bad class, and say what must be checked before subtraction is valid. Do not calculate the final number yet. In final synthesis, a method name is less important than a correct object model, justified hypotheses and a complete argument.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S16-T@1.scoredLearnerAction: Computes P(∅)={∅}. | States |P(∅)|=1. | Computes P({∅})={∅,{∅}}. | States |P({∅})|=2. | Explicitly distinguishes the empty set ∅ from the one-element set {∅}.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S16-T@1.classificationJustification: The prompt presents ∅ and {∅} but does not state the decisive distinction; the S16 guided check explicitly compares ∅ with {∅}, so that distinction is visibly rehearsed.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S17-T@1.decision: Reconstruct set operations from property-defined sets rather than two explicitly listed operand sets.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S17-T@1.scoredLearnerAction: Uses the verbal definitions to identify the union A∪B and lists {2,3,4,6,8,9,10,12}. | Identifies A∩B={6,12}. | Identifies A\B={2,4,8,10}. | Identifies A^c={1,3,5,7,9,11} relative to U. | Gives the corresponding cardinalities 8,2,4,6 and ties them to the defining membership conditions.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S17-T@1.classificationJustification: The prompt supplies property-defined sets (evens and multiples of 3), but S17 instruction works with explicitly listed sets. Reconstructing the members from properties is not visibly rehearsed.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S20-T@1.decision: Move from an explicitly tabulated mapping to a formula-defined map and reconstruct image/preimage/range.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S20-T@1.scoredLearnerAction: Finds the range {0,1,4}. | Computes g({−2,1})={4,1}. | Computes g⁻¹({1,4})={−2,−1,1,2}. | Identifies 9 as the unused codomain element. | Keeps image, preimage, range and codomain roles distinct.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S20-T@1.classificationJustification: The prompt supplies a formula-defined map g(x)=x² and asks image/preimage/range questions; S20 visible examples are explicit finite mapping tables, not formula-defined maps.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S21-T@1.decision: Move from bijection/inverse construction to collision + surjection and infer impossibility of a two-sided inverse.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S21-T@1.scoredLearnerAction: Identifies the collision g(1)=g(2)=a and correctly concludes g is not injective. | Shows both codomain values a and b are hit, so g is surjective. | Explains concretely why one inverse value at a cannot recover both original inputs 1 and 2. | Concludes that g is not bijective and has no two-sided inverse function.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S21-T@1.classificationJustification: The prompt asks to classify the supplied map and explain inverse failure but does not state collision+surjection as the diagnosis. S21 instruction rehearses injective-not-surjective and bijective cases, not this noninjective-surjective collision surface.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S23-T@1.decision: Choose product within two branches and addition across disjoint branches; the task no longer supplies the rule names.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S23-T@1.scoredLearnerAction: Counts Visitor badges as3·4=12 using sequential choices within that format. | Counts Staff badges as2·5=10 using sequential choices within that format. | Recognizes the two formats as disjoint alternatives rather than sequential stages. | Adds the branch totals to obtain22 badges. | Explains why multiplication applies within each format while addition combines the two disjoint formats.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S23-T@1.classificationJustification: The prompt supplies sequential choices and disjoint formats but does not name product-within/add-across as the organizing decision. S23 visibly rehearses exactly the sequential-versus-disjoint rule choice.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S24-T@1.decision: Recast ordered selection as counting injective functions from a labeled domain.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S24-T@1.scoredLearnerAction: Counts injective assignments sequentially as7·6·5. | Obtains the correct total210. | Expresses the same count as P(7,3). | Explains why previously used codomain values cannot be reused under injectivity. | Explains why the labeled domain elements a,b,c make the assignments ordered.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S24-T@1.classificationJustification: The public task explicitly supplies the injective-function representation and P(7,3); v1.7 S24 instruction deliberately contains only medals/roles, so the function-map recast is not rehearsed.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S25-T@1.decision: Handle a fixed-member constraint before applying labeled-group multinomial counting.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S25-T@1.scoredLearnerAction: Fixes student A in Morning before counting the remaining assignments. | Uses the remaining labeled group sizes3,3,2 to obtain the factorial quotient 8!/(3!3!2!). | Obtains the correct count560. | Explains why internal order within each shift does not create a new assignment and is divided out. | Explains why Morning, Afternoon and Night remain distinct labels and are not divided out.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S25-T@1.classificationJustification: The prompt states the fixed-member constraint (A must be in Morning), strongly cueing that constraint first. S25 factorial-grouping instruction contains no fixed-member example and does not rehearse the fix-A-first obstacle.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S27-T@1.decision: Recast a monomial's exponent vector as a nonnegative composition of total degree, then handle strict positivity by a lower-bound shift.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S27-T@1.scoredLearnerAction: Translates total degree10 into the nonnegative integer equation a+b+c+d=10. | Uses stars-and-bars to obtain C(13,3)=286 total-degree10 monomials. | Handles positive exponents by shifting each exponent down by1. | Counts the positive-exponent case as C(9,3)=84. | Explains the bijection between exponent vectors and stars-and-bars distributions.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S27-T@1.classificationJustification: The prompt explicitly asks for an exponent-vector↔stars-and-bars correspondence. S27 teaches stars-and-bars and lower-bound shifting, but does not rehearse the changed algebraic monomial/exponent-vector representation.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S28-T@1.decision: Recast two-set inclusion-exclusion from population categories to divisibility sets over integers.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S28-T@1.scoredLearnerAction: Counts multiples of 2 in 1..100 correctly. | Counts multiples of 5 in 1..100 correctly. | Identifies the overlap as multiples of 10. | Applies inclusion-exclusion to the divisibility-by-2-or-5 count. | Obtains the final union count 60.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S28-T@1.classificationJustification: The prompt explicitly requires inclusion-exclusion on divisibility by 2 or 5. S28 teaches inclusion-exclusion on listed/population sets, not the divisibility-set recast.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S29-T@1.decision: Invent the ten consecutive-pair holes; the decisive grouping is not supplied.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S29-T@1.scoredLearnerAction: Uses the eleven selected integers as pigeons. | Designs the ten consecutive-pair pigeonholes {1,2},{3,4},...,{19,20}. | Applies pigeonhole correctly to force two selected integers into one pair. | Concludes those two selected integers are consecutive. | Does not claim a particular pair is forced.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S29-T@1.classificationJustification: The prompt says only to design 10 pigeonholes; it does not supply the consecutive pairs {1,2},{3,4},…,{19,20}. Visible S29 instruction uses folders/drawers and does not rehearse that pair construction.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S30-T@1.decision: Choose an exact representation for onto functions, justify overlap/boundary corrections, and separately choose a fibre-capacity argument for the preimage guarantee.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S30-T@1.scoredLearnerAction: Counts 150 onto functions with justified correction, then proves a size-at-least-2 fibre exists and distinguishes guarantee from identity.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S30-T@1.classificationJustification: The prompt does not name inclusion–exclusion, define missing-output sets, give the correction signs or name pigeonhole. It demands the result and proof standards only.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S31-T@1.decision: Translate allowed-output sets into a dependent function for ∀∃ and into a common-intersection requirement for ∃∀.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S31-T@1.scoredLearnerAction: Constructs a legal f for all three inputs; exhaustively proves no one y lies in all three allowed sets; explains dependent versus global witness semantics.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S31-T@1.classificationJustification: The prompt supplies the finite relation but not the intersection criterion or the successful function. The learner must choose a representation that makes the quantifier order operational.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S32-T@1.decision: Use the domain restriction, not new algebra, as the decisive reason uniqueness changes.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S32-T@1.scoredLearnerAction: Finds two real roots, then proves only the nonnegative root survives on the restricted domain and explains the change in uniqueness.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S32-T@1.classificationJustification: The prompt names both domains but does not supply the factorization proof or the reason the negative solution is excluded. The meaningful change is the legality/domain obstacle.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S33-T@1.decision: Choose the least element of the finite set and use the closure rule to manufacture a smaller member.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S33-T@1.scoredLearnerAction: Justifies the finite minimum, applies the closure condition and contradicts minimality.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S33-T@1.classificationJustification: The prompt asks for an extremal element but does not provide which extremum or the contradiction move. The mathematical surface differs from the indexed least-counterexample proof.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S34-T@1.decision: Inspect fibre sizes rather than trusting the superficial three-marker symmetry.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S34-T@1.scoredLearnerAction: Computes the marked-string domain, identifies fibres, exhibits varying multiplicities and rejects the division before counting B correctly.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S34-T@1.classificationJustification: The prompt asks for an audit but does not tell the learner which fibres differ. The decisive step is discovering that multiplicity equals Hamming weight and therefore varies.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S35-T@1.decision: Invent a finite object with two nested membership states so C(4,k) chooses an outer set and 2^k chooses internal structure, then recast each element as one of three states.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S35-T@1.scoredLearnerAction: Defines a valid counted set, obtains the given summand by one partition and 81 by a different enumeration, and proves both counts are of the same set.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S35-T@1.classificationJustification: No incidence/nested-subset model is supplied in the prompt, and the lesson uses a person-team incidence rather than a binomial-power identity.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S36-M@1.decision: Reject the tempting but non-decisive sum invariant and choose a parity invariant that separates start from target.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S36-M@1.scoredLearnerAction: Finds a decisive preserved property, proves both move cases preserve it and uses its mismatch to rule out the target.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S36-M@1.classificationJustification: The prompt asks for an invariant but not which one; the easiest visible invariant x+y does not solve the task. The learner must make a mathematically consequential choice.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S36-T@1.decision: Choose one preserved quantity and a different decreasing integer quantity, then assign the correct conclusion to each.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S36-T@1.scoredLearnerAction: Proves a−b invariant, a+b decreasing integer rank, termination, terminal state and move count with role separation.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S36-T@1.classificationJustification: The prompt names the categories invariant/rank but does not supply the functions. Correct completion requires choosing quantities with different logical roles.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S30-M@1.decision: Choose a representation that counts total set membership and compare it with the maximum capacity under the negation of the target.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S30-M@1.scoredLearnerAction: Defines a finite membership representation, obtains 52, derives the at-most-48 contradiction under the negated target, and states existence-not-identity.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S30-M@1.classificationJustification: The prompt gives no method name, incidence set, average formula or pigeonhole partition. Visible instruction uses binary strings/committees, not a family-of-subsets capacity guarantee.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S01@1.wrongApproach: Treat R(r) as already true/false without assigning r.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S01@1.requiredDiscrimination: Rubric requires identifying the free variable and open predicate.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S02@1.requiredDiscrimination: The (T,T) interpretation of inclusive OR is explicitly scored.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S03@1.requiredDiscrimination: Separate rubric rows require both forms and their relationship.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S04@1.wrongApproach: Prove only one direction and declare iff.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S05@1.requiredDiscrimination: Domain-consistency and domain-effect explanation are scored.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S06@1.wrongApproach: Negate a universal without switching to an existential, or negate >0 as <0 instead of ≤0.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S06@1.requiredDiscrimination: Quantifier switch and inequality complement are separately scored.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S07@1.wrongApproach: Stop after a legal counterexample, or propose a corrected statement and support it only with more examples.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S07@1.requiredDiscrimination: Main observes legal strategic refutation; Transfer separately scores a boundary-preserving repair and an arbitrary-real proof of the repair.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S08@1.wrongApproach: Write 3|(n−1) as n−1=3 without an integer witness.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S08@1.requiredDiscrimination: Witness equations and integer witnesses are explicitly scored.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S09@1.wrongApproach: Conclude em is even without producing the integer witness.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S09@1.requiredDiscrimination: Final witness km is explicitly required.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S10@1.wrongApproach: Try to prove the original implication directly while assuming |x|<1.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S10@1.requiredDiscrimination: Rubric requires the actual contrapositive and valid real squaring step.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S11@1.wrongApproach: Assume N is greatest but fail to establish N+1 is an integer larger than N.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S12@1.wrongApproach: Check a few residues/numerical examples without proving exhaustive cases.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S12@1.requiredDiscrimination: Rubric requires general remainder form, exhaustive parity and universal recombination.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S13@1.wrongApproach: Verify several n values but omit induction hypothesis/step.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S13@1.requiredDiscrimination: Base, IH and k→k+1 step are separate scoring obligations.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S14@1.wrongApproach: Use P(k−2) without an all-prior hypothesis or sufficient bases.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S14@1.requiredDiscrimination: Rubric explicitly checks all-prior access and noncircular reduction.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S15@1.wrongApproach: Confuse element membership with subset inclusion.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S15@1.requiredDiscrimination: Separate requested statements force membership/subset/equality distinctions.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S16@1.wrongApproach: Treat ∅ and {∅} as the same set.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S16@1.requiredDiscrimination: Their distinct power sets/cardinalities are explicit scored outputs.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S17@1.wrongApproach: List sets by guesswork but use complement relative to the wrong universe.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S17@1.requiredDiscrimination: A^c is explicitly relative to U and property-based reasoning is required.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S18@1.wrongApproach: Verify only the finite example and treat it as proof.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S18@1.requiredDiscrimination: Rubric requires arbitrary-element iff proof and separately labels the finite case as a check.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S19@1.wrongApproach: Call R a function because it is a relation or because it has three pairs.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S19@1.requiredDiscrimination: Rubric requires exact one-output-per-input diagnosis, including the missing input3 output.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S20@1.wrongApproach: Treat g⁻¹({1,4}) as reciprocal values or as an inverse function.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S20@1.requiredDiscrimination: Rubric requires the actual preimage subset of the domain.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S21@1.wrongApproach: Call the collision map bijective because every codomain value is hit.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S21@1.requiredDiscrimination: Rubric separately checks collision/noninjectivity and inverse impossibility.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S22@1.wrongApproach: List residue classes without verifying reflexive/symmetric/transitive.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S22@1.requiredDiscrimination: All three relation properties and the resulting partition are scored.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S23@1.wrongApproach: Multiply all four branch/stage counts together.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S23@1.requiredDiscrimination: Rubric requires product within each format and addition across disjoint formats.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S24@1.wrongApproach: Use 7^3 and allow repeated codomain values.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S25@1.wrongApproach: Divide out the shift labels or forget the fixed student A.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S25@1.requiredDiscrimination: Rubric separately checks fixed-first logic, internal-order division and retained labels.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S26@1.wrongApproach: Copy only the n=5 expansion without stating the general theorem/coefficient argument.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S26@1.requiredDiscrimination: General theorem production, combinatorial coefficient reason and fresh expansion are independently scored.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S27@1.wrongApproach: Count ordered strings of variables or treat the exponents as distinguishable tokens instead of an exponent vector satisfying one sum constraint.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S27@1.requiredDiscrimination: Rubric requires the exponent equation, stars-and-bars count, positive shift and explicit exponent-vector bijection.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S28@1.requiredDiscrimination: The overlap and correction are explicit rubric obligations.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S29@1.wrongApproach: Use the ten residues mod10 as holes, which does not force consecutive values.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S29@1.requiredDiscrimination: Transfer rubric requires the consecutive-pair hole design.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S30@1.wrongApproach: Wait for a named method, count local pieces without showing they refer to the same universe, subtract missed-output cases without restoring overlaps, or say 'some fibre is large' without a capacity proof.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S30@1.requiredDiscrimination: Main requires an explicit representation plus 52-versus-48 guarantee; Transfer requires an exact overlap-aware onto count and a logically separate fibre-capacity existence proof.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S31@1.wrongApproach: Choose a different y for each x while claiming this proves ∃y∀x, or swap the quantifier symbols without negating the predicate.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S31@1.requiredDiscrimination: Main requires one fixed m for the ∃∀ reading and exact nested negation; Transfer requires either one common y or an exhaustive proof none exists.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S32@1.wrongApproach: Find one candidate and declare it unique, or factor x²=16 and forget to apply the stated domain.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S32@1.requiredDiscrimination: Main separately scores two-solution uniqueness; Transfer separately scores the domain-based exclusion of −4.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S33@1.wrongApproach: Say 'let N be the smallest counterexample' without defining a nonempty integer set, or assume arbitrary positive-real sets have minima.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S33@1.requiredDiscrimination: Main scores the counterexample-set/well-ordering prerequisites and the explicit positive-real counterexample to the false minimum rule.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S34@1.wrongApproach: Divide a labelled/marked count by the number of possible labels without checking that every output has that many preimages.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S34@1.requiredDiscrimination: Transfer rubric requires explicit unequal fibre sizes and rejects the divide-by-three shortcut.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S35@1.wrongApproach: Expand both sides numerically or manipulate the binomial theorem without defining one set that both sides count.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S35@1.requiredDiscrimination: Both Main and Transfer rubrics explicitly require a single finite set, two decompositions and exact-once counting.

T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S36@1.wrongApproach: Use the preserved sum in Main even though it agrees at the target, or claim that any decreasing quantity proves finite termination and that termination identifies the terminal state.
T22V3::T22E-DISC01::S36@1.requiredDiscrimination: Main marking rejects sum-alone as decisive; Transfer separately scores an integer rank, termination, and invariant-based terminal-state identification.
